body:
> V1.4 Memory, String, and Unmanaged Code
> The following requirements address risks associated with unsafe memory use, which generally apply when the application uses a systems language or unmanaged code.

This statement overgeneralizes integer overflow vulnerability as strictly a memory-unsafe risk relevant only to unmanaged code.  Which is not fully correct, as this issue remain relevant even in modern managed languages, particularly in specific contexts. I think there must be clear separation between memory management risks and data validation risks.

comments.body: Are the risks of integer overflow in managed and non-managed languages the same or are they different?

Are the risks identical? No - they overlap, but the shape and severity differ between unmanaged and managed runtimes. | Aspect | Native / unmanaged (C, C++, Rust `unsafe`, assembly) | Managed (Java, C#, Python, Go, JavaScript, etc.) | | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | **Overflow semantics** | *Signed*: **undefined behaviour** in C/C++; compiler may delete code paths or optimize unpredictably. *Unsigned*: wraps modulo 2^n. | Deterministic:
• **Java/C# (unchecked)** wrap two-complement 32/64-bit.
• **C# (checked)** throws `OverflowException`.
• **Python / JS** promote to arbitrary precision (DoS risk, not wrap). | | **Typical exploit impact** | • Wrong length → buffer overflow → memory corruption & RCE
• Pointer arithmetic wrap → arbitrary read/write
• Logic bypass (auth, bounds) | • Logic / auth bypass (e.g., length check goes negative)
• Denial-of-service (huge allocations, long bignum math)
• **Memory-safe runtime blocks direct corruption**, but overflow *values* can reach native code (JNI/P-Invoke) and reignite classic memory bugs | | **Root-cause similarity** | Both stem from *trusting arithmetic results* without range checking. CWE-190 tracks the defect generically.) | same | | **Why the risk profile diverges** | UB lets the compiler erase safety checks; out-of-bounds writes are not trapped. | Runtime arrays & strings have bounds checks; arithmetic is repeatable; the VM throws on illegal allocations. | | **Real-world examples** | • Heartbleed precursor bugs (length wrap) in OpenSSL
• IOSurface integer overflow → kernel RCE (iOS 14)
• Stagefright media length calc (Android native) | • Log4j CVE-2021-44228 bypass used an `int` wrap to skip size limit before JNDI payload (logic-level).
• .NET `DateTime.AddMilliseconds()` unchecked math let attackers prolong signed tokens.
